opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's evolved quite a bit. Early on, I think a lot of us assumed the answer was simply "make the context window bigger." If you could fit everything in, the model would just figure it out. And longer context really has gotten much better, so for a lot of tasks, dumping the relevant documents straight in works well.

But what I've come to appreciate is that it isn't really an either-or. Putting everything in context has costs. It's slower and more expensive, and even when a model *can* attend to a huge amount of text, it doesn't always attend to the right parts. Important details can get diluted by a lot of irrelevant material. Search, on the other hand, lets the model be deliberate. It can decide what it needs, go get it, look at what came back, and then refine the query. That's much closer to how a skilled person actually does research.

The bigger shift in my thinking came from seeing models get better at *using* tools in a multi-step way. When search was a single retrieval call bolted onto the front of a prompt, it was brittle. If the first retrieval missed, you were stuck. Now models can reason about what they're missing, search again, cross-check sources, and notice contradictions. That makes search feel less like a workaround for limited context and more like a core capability.

So where I've landed is roughly this: context is great for information you know is relevant and want the model to hold in mind as a whole, like a codebase you're working in or a document you're analyzing closely. Search is better when the space of possibly relevant information is huge, changing, or unknown in advance, which describes most of the real world. The interesting work now is in evaluating how well models combine the two: knowing when to rely on what's already in front of them and when to go looking for more.

r001.rationale: The response says putting everything in context is slower and more expensive, then describes search as a deliberate way to retrieve what the model needs and says it is better for huge information spaces.

r002.rationale: It identifies search as useful for huge information spaces and describes it as a way to address limited context, communicating that search can reach information beyond what fits directly in the context window.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's shifted a lot. A couple of years ago, I think I had this pretty strong intuition that if you could just get the information into context, you should. Retrieval felt like a hack, something you did because context windows were short, and the dream was that windows would get long enough that you'd just dump everything in and let the model sort it out.

What actually changed my mind was watching how models behave when they're evaluated on real tasks, as opposed to toy ones. A lot of my work has been on evals, and one thing you see over and over is that a model with everything in context doesn't necessarily use it well. There's this gap between "the information is technically present" and "the model actually attends to the right part and reasons from it." Long context helps, but it doesn't automatically close that gap. Sometimes it makes things worse, because the model gets distracted by the stuff that's irrelevant.

And then on the other side, search started looking less like a crutch and more like a skill. When a model has to decide what to look for, formulate a query, read the result, and then decide whether it's got enough or needs to look again, that's a loop. And that loop is doing real work. It forces a kind of prioritization that just stuffing context doesn't. The model has to form a hypothesis about what it needs. When it works, you get something that feels closer to how a person researches a question, iteratively, rather than reading the whole library first.

So where I've landed is that it's not really an either-or. For a lot of problems, the right thing is both. You want enough in context that the model has grounding and doesn't go searching for things it should already know, and you want tools so it can go get what it's missing. The interesting design question becomes where the boundary is. What belongs in the prompt, what belongs behind a tool call, and how do you evaluate whether the model is making good decisions about when to reach for the tool.

That last part is the one I find myself thinking about most. If you're grading only the final answer, you can't tell whether the model got there by reasoning well or by luck. You actually want to look at the trajectory. Did it search for sensible things, did it stop when it had enough, did it notice when a result contradicted what it already believed. Those are the behaviors that generalize, and they're also the ones that are hardest to measure.

r001.rationale: The response says search can prioritize relevant information and avoid distraction from irrelevant context, but does not clearly state that search is more efficient than putting all available information in context.

r002.rationale: The response says tools can retrieve what the model is missing, but does not clearly connect that to accessing information beyond the context window’s capacity.

astra-6.text:
I’ve moved away from thinking of it as an either-or choice. Putting everything in context is appealing because the model has all the information right there. But a larger context isn’t automatically a better context—you still have to figure out what’s relevant.

Search gives the model a way to pull in information as it needs it. The tradeoff is that it has to know what to look for, and it can miss something important. So I think the interesting question is: what should the model have up front, and what should it be able to go find? Give it enough context to understand the task, then let it search for the details that help it make progress.

r001.rationale: The response says search can retrieve information as needed and that more context is not automatically better, but it does not state that this approach is more efficient than placing all available information in context.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that search provides access to information beyond what fits in the model’s context window.

sol-6.1.text:
I’ve become less convinced that it’s an either-or decision. Putting information directly into context can be really useful when you know what’s relevant and you want the model to reason across all of it. But a larger context window doesn’t necessarily mean you should put everything in there. You still have to decide what belongs, and you can end up adding a lot of noise.

Search gives the model a way to get information as it needs it. The interesting challenge then becomes whether it knows what to search for, whether it can recognize a useful result, and whether it knows when it has enough information to answer.

So I think more about the combination now: give the model enough context to understand the task, and let it search for the additional details it needs along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says search can retrieve additional details as needed and can reduce noise, but it does not state that this is more efficient than putting all available information in context.

r002.rationale: The response mentions context windows but does not say search provides access to information beyond what can fit in them.
